speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-PRESS REPORT RESPECTING DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister? Would the Prime Minister care to comment on the Canadian Press dispatch, of which I have sent him a copy, in which a provincial premier states that the federal government last July rejected a request that a dominion-provincial conference be called to deal with unemployment?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-PRESS REPORT RESPECTING DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I note that the Canadian Press report referred to in the question does not quote Premier Bennett's actual words and I am therefore somewhat reluctant to make any comment. However, the premier of British Columbia did write to me on July 14 last on the subject of the provision of assistance for unemployed employables, and in his letter he stated that "the wisdom of holding a federal-provincial conference may commend itself to you".
While this could hardly be construed as a request for such a conference the government, in its reply to the premier, stated that it felt that the provision of unemployment insurance and other measures by the federal government relieved the burden of the provision of relief of the unemployed to the point where provinces and municipalities could carry out their constitutional responsibilities in_ that connection.

maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-PRESS REPORT RESPECTING DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
In view of the delegations that are appearing every day in parliament on this important matter I should like to ask a supplementary question of the Prime Minister. Will the government give consideration to calling immediately a dominion-provincial conference to work out the division of costs between the federal, provincial and municipal governments for providing for unemployed employables who have no entitlement to unemployment insurance benefits?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this matter of unemployment-which is one that is, I am sure, seriously regretted by all hon. members -is receiving constant consideration.

speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice. Is the minister aware that a pamphlet entitled "Crime in your Community" has been published by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and distributed throughout Canada? Is the minister aware of the fact that the 50,000 copies printed and distributed were all in English? speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
subtopic: FRENCH COPIES OF PAMPHLET
speechtext:
I wish to thank the hon. member for Quebec West for having given me notice of his question. The pamphlet in question was produced by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to inform citizens as to how they might better guard their property against criminals. The pamphlet has been given general distribution only in those parts of Canada in which the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, acting under contract as either the provincial or municipal police force, have the responsibility for the enforcement of the general body of the criminal law. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police do not have that responsibility either in the province of Ontario or Quebec which have their own provincial police forces, or in those municipalities in which the primary responsibility for policing and law enforcement is that of the municipal police force. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police therefore have not made a general distribution of the pamphlet either in the provinces of Ontario or Quebec or in these municipalities to which I have referred. Copies of the pamphlet, however, have been sent as a matter of information to the Ontario, Quebec and these municipal police forces and to the press.
In the eight provinces of Canada and in the municipalities in which the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are the only police force, large quantities of this pamphlet have been sent to every Royal Canadian Mounted Police detachment with instructions to get the pamphlet into the hands of those who could make good use of the suggestions contained in them. A French version of the pamphlet has been in preparation and will be available next week. Meanwhile it has

been possible to provide copies of the French version in typescript form pending the printing of the same.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. My question arises out of the report on the T.C.A. accident near Brampton on December 17, 1954. In view of the fact that T.C.A. in many instances operates under regulations more strict than those required by the air regulations under the Aeronautics Act, will consideration be given to avoiding pilots having to be on duty on domestic lines for as long as 16 hours a day?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext: There is no foundation for the suggestion that pilots on domestic services are on duty for 16 hours. It is not the case. The official report is the report of those duly appointed to carry out the duty of investigating the accident. The commission included three very competent experts, and also a medical board. The report of both these boards was included in the report to the minister. There is no suggestion that I can find in the report that the T.C.A. officers were on duty 16 hours a day, and my knowledge of the situation indicates that is not the case.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question? I realize I cannot argue with the minister's statement, but the report on which my question was based is a matter of record. Is he making it clear, however, that as a general practice there are no terms of duty of 16 hours a day on T.C.A.?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext: The rules are well established. I suppose if a flight to England were delayed by headwinds there might be a term of duty as long as 16 hours, but certainly there would be one or two days lay-off following it. The rules of T.C.A. are well established. They are made by agreement with the pilots' association, and I do not think my hon. friend could suggest any changes that would improve the situation.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. This afternoon on the orders of the day I asked a question of the Minister of Trade and Commerce which I indicated was based on a report of the Trans-Canada Air Lines accident at Brampton on December 17, 1954. Arising out of that report, I asked a question about a term of duty as long as 16 hours a day. The Minister of Trade and Commerce replied to the effect that there was no foundation for the suggestion that pilots are on duty for 16 hours. He


went on and referred to the three-man report to which I had referred, stating there was no suggestion he could find in the report that officers were on duty for 16 hours a day.
On a matter of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I wish to place on the record just one paragraph from the report to which I referred, which will make it clear-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext: This is not privilege, this is argument.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext: It was said by the minister that there was no foundation in the report for my question. All I wish to do, Mr. Speaker, is place on the record one paragraph from the report.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext: I can see that there are some doubts as to the propriety of putting this quotation on the record at this time. It is true that the minister concerned is not here at the moment, but I take it the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is indicating that he wants to justify the question he put, that is the veracity of his assertion-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext: Correct.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext: I am at a loss to find anything which is derogatory so far as our rules are concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext: On the point of order, or privilege, I have never understood that an hon. member could, on a point of privilege, insert into the record something which would justify a statement he may have made. Privilege is reserved for the explanation of what he himself may have said at one time or another, or what he did not say. But it is not a process of the house in which, a member having said one thing, and someone else having denied it, he will attempt to justify it, unless it is within the peculiar knowledge and with respect to the person of the member himself.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext:
The hon. member asked a question which he says was based upon a report. He could not, in a question on the orders of the day, quote from the report. The minister who answered the question said there was no foundation in the report to justify the allegation made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
Now, if the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre can further justify that there were good grounds for having put the question in the way he did, then he clears the position up, so far as he is concerned. Otherwise what is the implication? The implication is that the hon. member was not telling the truth.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext: Oh, no.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext: I think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext: Surely not.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext:
Well, if that is not so, I must say that I do not wish in this case to give any special privilege to anyone. I am just trying to be fair to the hon. member. But apparently the attitude he is now taking does not appeal to many hon. members in the house.
It may be that he could find another opportunity to make good his claim that the question he asked, based upon a report, was exactly as he construed it. Of course the only ground I can find for refusing permission to the hon. member to proceed at this time is that he wants to give further explanation of a question he has put; and we must keep in mind that when questions are asked on the orders of the day they are open to that kind of risk. Because an hon. member, when asking his question, can give no more information than is absolutely necessary for such purpose.
The hon. member has done that and he has had an answer. What remains I think must become a debatable point between the hon. member and the Minister of Trade and Commerce on a later occasion. The hon. member may have to offer it as a grievance on a motion to go into supply, or he may speak when the estimates of the Department of Transport are being considered, and when there is discussion of salaries of Trans-Canada Air Lines employees, at which time the working conditions can be discussed generally. At that time the hon. member may make a point of it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext:
I would point out with
respect, Mr. Speaker, that earlier in your remarks you indicated what was my point of privilege, namely that my veracity had been called into question in respect of a statement I had made earlier.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext: I do not wish to argue the question. I wish merely to put on the record the statement contained in the report on the basis of which I founded my question. I would not be asking to do this had it not been that the minister said there was no foundation for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext: He did not say that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext: This is not a matter of requiring unanimous consent; it is a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext:
Other hon. members object to the course the hon. member wishes to follow. The hon. member had the report before him, and the point could have been taken up immediately following the question which was put. If he had spoken at that time on a question of privilege, to clarify his
Canada Elections Act
position, I am sure he would have had permission from the house. But several hours have elapsed since that time. I think the hon. member's position will not be prejudiced if he waits until a little later to do what he wants to do.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext: I am prepared to let it go with just a word. I think Your Honour will understand that it was difficult at that time for me to thumb through all the pages of this report to find a certain paragraph, even though I knew it was there. But it is there, at page 15-the reference to 16 hours on duty in one day.

maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext: It is unfair that this implication should be left. I was in the house when the minister answered the question, and he said that, if a pilot did work such hours on any one flight, he had from two to three days off, and the inference was that they were not overfatigued because of the flight on that particular day. He told us that there was no foundation for saying that the pilot was overfatigued. He did not suggest there was no foundation for the statement that he worked 16 hours a day.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext: He most certainly did.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext: Well, this may be a good indication that many questions asked on the orders of the day in the form in which they are asked should not be asked.

maintopic: AVOIDANCE OF LONG HOURS OF DUTY FOR PILOTS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, we welcome the opportunity to make an examination of the Canada Elections Act. We believe it is worth while doing so at this stage, when perhaps an election is not just around the corner. Naturally at this moment we are a bit in the dark as to the nature of the amendments that will be placed before the committee; but, coming as they will in large measure from the chief electoral officer, in whom we have confidence, we would expect that as a result of those amendments considerable improvement would be made in the elections act.
I have in mind a number of matters connected with the act, and naturally we will see whether the amendments proposed by the chief electoral officer cover those items. I am somewhat surprised however that at this particular stage, when introducing the motion, the minister has come along with an amendment extending greatly the investigations to be carried out by the committee. I am not sure that this implies on his part anything in the nature of careful preparation, when he places a motion on the order paper and then, on the occasion when it is brought to the attention of the house, offers an amendment. Particularly is this so when the amendment deals with the very broad question of redistribution which, naturally, would involve
Canada Elections Act
more extensive work on the part of the committee than is implied by the motion now before us.
However I think hon. members will welcome an opportunity to discuss the problem of redistribution in perhaps a quieter atmosphere than prevailed when we were on the subject not so long ago.
I would say in conclusion-because until we see the measure we cannot debate it at length-that the general working out of the elections act under the supervision of the chief electoral officer has met with approval. As I said, we have confidence in him. We like the idea of having him as an appointee of parliament in general, and we recognize the fact that he is not under any obligation to any one party in the house. This sets above party consideratiofts the actual operation of the elections act and the carrying out of the duties of the chief electoral officer. We will await with interest the actual details of the measure.

Mr. Speaker, we welcome the decision of the government to have the elections act referred to the committee. I believe that for some years it has been the practice to set up a special committee, whereas now the proposal is to have the matter referred to the standing committee on privileges and elections. Nothing seems to turn on that, and perhaps this is a good time to make use of a standing committee which has not met too often in the last few years.
As the Secretary of State is aware, there are likely to be a number of other suggestions made which the committee might consider. Some of them may come from members speaking to this resolution today, and others will be made by members serving on the standing committee.
I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) that the election machinery of this country is in good hands, in the person of the chief electoral officer, Mr. Nelson Castonguay. We all have great confidence in this appointee of the House of Commons, and we know that any suggestions he brings to the committee involving changes in the elections act will be changes that he feels, out of his experience in the last election, should be made. I hope the same consideration for proposed changes will be accorded to the suggestions made by members as I know members will accord to the suggestions to be made by Mr. Castonguay.
Mr. Speaker, it is not my purpose to speak at length. Indeed, if I may say so, the Secretary of State (Mr. Pinard) has cut considerably shorter than otherwise would have been

the case the remarks I had intended to make, by the amendment to the motion he has had one of his colleagues move.
We are glad to note the decision of the government that it will be appropriate for the committee to discuss various means of adjusting the representation in the boundaries of constituencies represented in the House of Commons. In the action he has taken today, he has corrected a fault of the last session. The Secretary of State has referred to the fact that the motion of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), as amended, passed at the last session. But for some of us it was a matter of annoyance that, though the amended motion passed, nothing was done about it throughout the remainder of the session. The committee named in the amendment simply did not meet. [DOT]
Most of us recall the excellent speech the esteemed member for Quebec South made on the question of redistribution on December 7, 1953. At the end of that speech he said, as reported at page 669 of Hansard for that date:
I have heard it said that parliament is capable of great things, of carrying on its business with dignity, decorum, fairness and impartiality, but that when it comes to decisions with respect to redistribution it falls far short of that which the people of Canada expect from it. It seems to me we can now make a study of this matter coolly, calmly and with great deliberation, and thus do some good to ourselves and to the people of Canada. I commend such a study to this house.
I am sorry it has taken this long for a committee of the house to get authority to carry out that study. However I am glad it is going to be made, and I hope it will be carried on in the vein suggested by the hon. member for Quebec South, when he made this proposal at the last session of parliament. In this connection, Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out once again, as I did on January 19, 1955, by means of a question on the orders of the day to the Secretary of State (Mr. Pinard), that in my own province of Manitoba a decision has just about been concluded to provide for redistribution in Manitoba, so far as provincial electoral boundaries are concerned, by an independent commission. A very important committee has been working on this matter for a number of months. It has made a report to the Manitoba provincial legislature recommending quite a number of electoral changes. One of the proposed changes is that the electoral boundaries in the province of Manitoba be drawn up henceforth by an independent commission. I hope that the lead which is thus being given by the province of Manitoba will soon be followed by this parliament, and I hope that serious study will be given by this committee to the proposals laid before the legislature of Manitoba in the report to which I have referred.

I would not want the Secretary of State or the committee to get the impression that I agree with everything that is in the report that has been presented to the Manitoba legislature. For example, I think the ratio that it establishes as between urban and rural seats on a 7 to 4 basis is much wider than it should be, and it is much wider than was proposed by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) when he dealt with this matter some time ago, but that issue is not before us. I just wanted to indicate that in commending to this committee a study of the report made in Manitoba I was not commending everything in it, but was commending in particular the proposal that redistribution be done by an independent commission.
I think we have all listened with great attention to the pleas that have been made to us from time to time in this matter by the hon. member for Quebec South, and I think we shall be doing a good day's work for democracy and for Canada when we make a real improvement in the matter of redistribution, when we take it out of political control and provide for it to be brought about on the basis of an independent commission. I hope that this matter will receive the study it deserves; I hope the comi mittee will have an entirely free hand to give full consideration to all the suggestions that will be made in that committee by various members, to the end that we might still further improve our election machinery in this country.

Mr. Chairman, as the text of the resolution indicates, the purpose of the bill is to increase the number of members of the national harbours board from three to four. The substantial growth in traffic and
1510	HOUSE OF
National Harbours Board Act earnings of the national harbours board since it was constituted in 1936 has been accompanied by a corresponding increase in its responsibilities. Total cargo tonnage has risen by 73 per cent and the total revenues are three times greater than in 1935. The number of vessels entering national ports is also much higher.
With the increase in use of our national harbours greater responsibilities rest upon the board to determine the adequacy of facilities, to plan for future development and in general administration. I am sure that hon. members will agree that the operation of such a body as the national harbours board can be efficient and satisfactory only to the degree that the board is fully cognizant of actual conditions and local problems in each of the ports under its jurisdiction.
It is the view of the government that the proposed increase in membership will not only enable the board to keep pace with the growth of its responsibilities but will also permit more frequent visits to the ports to be made by individual members and by the board itself. In this way we believe that more numerous and better opportunities will be afforded for closer contact with the communities served by the national harbours.
I may conclude by saying that there are eight harbours under the jurisdiction of the board: Montreal, Vancouver, Churchill, Three Rivers, Quebec, Chicoutimi, Halifax and Saint John, New Brunswick. The board also is responsible for the operation of grain elevators at Port Colborne and Prescott.
I should like to add that I feel that enlargement of the board will enable it to render even more effective service in the communities served by the harbours under its jurisdiction.

speechtext:
I agree with the hon. member who has applauded that the chairman is an excellent civil servant and over the years has done fine work for the board. I believe the vice-chairman is Brigadier Archer of Quebec city. There is no representative from the west coast and I submit that the time has come when one member of this board should be from the west coast. I believe that the port of Vancouver has far more ships plying in and out of the harbour than any other

COMMONS	.
national harbour. We are much further removed from Ottawa than any of the other harbours and it is of the utmost importance that there should be someone from the west coast on this board.
About a month ago a dispatch appeared in one of the Vancouver papers to the effect that there would be two new appointments, one from the west coast and the other an expert in the grain trade, the latter appointment being considered necessary because of the importance of the handling of grain in most of these ports. I am not in a position to say whether it is essential that there should be an expert on grain problems on the board, but certainly there should be a west coast man as member of the national harbours board.
The second suggestion I wish to place before the minister has to do with the point he himself stressed, namely, the contact of the board with local problems. The minister stated that the business through these ports had increased greatly in recent years, which of course is true. They have been filling a larger and larger place in the life of the nation. He also said that if one more man was added to the board it would help the board to become better acquainted with local problems. That may help to a degree but the thing that would really help the national harbours board to come to grips with local problems would be to have a local advisory committee in each port.
During each session for many years I have asked that such committees be set up but I have not been able to make much headway for some reason or other. The desire seems to be to hold all the strings right here in Ottawa; there must be complete control here in Ottawa. I hope I can take it from the minister's opening remarks today that that policy is not to be continued and that an attempt is to be made to keep the board in much closer touch with the local problems in the ports than it has been to date.
I would refer the minister to the well-known report by Sir Alexander Gibb on the national harbours of Canada made in 1932 and entitled "National Ports Survey". It was on the basis of this report that the national harbours board was set up in the first place, but the government did not follow his recommendation with regard to this extremely important point of maintaining some contact with local conditions in the ports. I refer the minister to page 30 of Sir Alexander Gibb's report under the heading of "Proposed Form of Control and Administration. Local Control". The first paragraph deals with the proposal that port managers be appointed, and of course that suggestion

was implemented in the legislation which followed. But with regard to local conditions Sir Alexander had this to say:
83.	Considerable latitude should be allowed to the port managers so long as their activities are directed to carrying out the policy laid down by the central authority. It is essential to avoid emasculating the local administration, since no centralized control can replace an efficient and active local administration, or the special knowledge and initiative of the local business community, both of which are vital to a port's prosperity.
84.	For this latter reason I strongly advocate a local advisory council. There are very many aspects of port working which such a council can properly care for, such as the representation of the interests of private wharf owners, of local merchants and distributors, of local consignees and exporters, of the labour view and of the attitude of boards of trade, chambers of commerce, corn exchanges and other such trade organizations, in addition to shipping.
Within recent months in Vancouver we have had a very good example of the part that could be played by a local committee. The fight to get the price of wheat at Vancouver back on a comparative basis with the price at Fort William and Port Arthur was led by two of the local unions. They were worried about the loss of employment. They went to great trouble to work out a brief and to make submissions urging that a change be made in government policy. They were able to rally behind them all of the business interests having to do with the ports. That was an example of a problem which affected Vancouver and which could be adequately emphasized only by some local body in that city. Sir Alexander Gibb went on to say this:
It serves very usefully to identify the community with the port;-
Being a member from the island of Montreal, the minister knows just how important that is. Sir Alexander Gibb continues:
-and to secure the support and interest of local members of parliament, the city council, or provincial government in schemes, and so anticipate and meet criticisms from any such quarters or action that might be prejudicial to the port. '
It is invaluable in exploring the possibilities of local markets, in carrying out advertisement and propaganda and in co-operation with interests likely to promote industrial developments. Finally a local council provides a useful check on the tendency of more or less permanent officials to become stereotyped or arbitrary.
That is, of course, one of the weaknesses in the present system. Today we have a national harbours board and a local manager in each port. He deals directly with the national harbours board. He does not need to worry much about what the business interests, labour interests, the city council or the other people in a port think about the developments in that port. He has only to deal with Ottawa. That set-up, I submit to
National Harbours Board Act the minister, is not the best possible one. Sir Alexander went on to say:
85.	The port manager would be ex-officio chairman of the council, which would meet regularly and be consulted on all such matters as proposed developments, alterations in rates, important changes in operation. The members of the council should have the right of initiating discussions on matters of policy affecting the port, on any complaints raised by users of the port, and on questions of rates, charges, etc.; but not on any purely executive matters, and they would have no executive duties or powers.
The advisory council's proceedings and recommendations would be submitted to the central authority, and they should have the right of direct access to the central authority, but not to any other department of government.
In the Montreal papers I have been reading about the concern felt in that great city about the changes that will be required because of the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway. Some interests in Montreal at least seem to be much worried about whether their port facilities are going to be brought up to date in time to take full advantage of the opening of the seaway. They are worried lest, if these facilities are not brought up to date, some other port may get the business. The minister has there at his own front door a good example of the benefits that could follow from the setting up of a local advisory council.
It is true that in two of the ports there are informal committees, or there were last year. I think one was in Halifax and the other in Quebec city. I am not sure of that but the former minister of transport, in answer to a question, told me that there were two informal committees. Instead of just providing for an additional member of the national harbours board, I hope the minister will take one step further and provide for these local advisory councils. For many years the Vancouver Sun has pleaded for action of this kind. As a matter of fact, I have here an extract from an editorial they wrote in 1932 at the time the Gibb report was first published. In it they had this to say:
Vancouver wants and needs and must have not less control but more control of her own affairs. Vancouver's port is the west's and Vancouver's way out to the world. Its control must stay in Vancouver.
By establishment of the national harbours board Vancouver lost control over the harbour. Now, more pier and wharf facilities are needed! machinery at docks needs replacing, the government system needs much overhaul to modernize it, investigation should be made into the N H B's efficiency here.
In reprinting this editorial the Sun had this to say:
Occasional visits to Vancouver_
The minister has emphasized today that there perhaps could be more visits if he had more men. I am saying that visits are not
1512	HOUSE OF
National Harbours Board Act enough. We want somebody out there who has the authority to sit in, to know what is being done and to make suggestions for improvement. The editorial continues:
-by the three-man N.H.B. aren't likely to produce these things. They haven't done much since 1933.
A competent local advisory council with the interests of the port at heart could get action. And if it spent time looking into the port's activities it might find plenty to get action about.
Those are my two suggestions for the minister today. Before he brings this bill to the house for second reading I hope he will give consideration to the second suggestion, the implementation of which I think will require a further amendment to the National Harbours Boards Act. I refer, of course, to the provision for local advisory councils. As to our port of Vancouver, may I say-and the same is true of Montreal, although perhaps not to the same extent, and it is certainly true of Halifax and Saint John-that our ports are vital to the development of the cities and the areas around the cities. These ports need the most progressive type of leadership. I believe that leadership can be achieved only if the local people are given a part in the direction of port activities.

I should like to try to reply briefly to some of the comments that have
National Harbours Board Act been made during the discussion of the resolution. I think hon. members will realize from what has been said how difficult it would be to satisfy all of the views that have been expressed today. There are those who believe that the maritimes should have representation, that Quebec should have representation, that the middle west should have representation and, in turn, that Vancouver should have representation. I find that it is not long before the number of available appointments runs out without everybody having been satisfied.
I think, however, that when one reflects for a moment one realizes two things concerning these appointments. The first is that while a commissioner may originate from a particular part of Canada such as the maritimes or the west coast, when he moves to Ottawa, as necessarily he must as a member of the national harbours board, he does after a time lose the rather close association with the place from which he came that existed at the time of his appointment. I do not think that members should be under illusions as to what I might describe as territorial representation. I think that territorial representation is in fact and in practice of rather brief duration. I believe that so far as possible we should look for the people who are best able to render the type of service that we expect from the members of the board, and that in making our choice we should try to find the talent and also give representation to various parts of Canada. I may assure hon. members that when the making of these appointments is considered we shall endeavour to compress the incompressible and to satisfy all the territorial recommendations that have been made, bearing in mind that our prime purpose is to have a board that is staffed with capable members who will be able to discharge fully the duties they are called upon to discharge under the statute.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, I think, spoke of the Gibb report and the question of local advisory committees. I may say I was not unfamiliar with the recommendation, and I understand that the matter has been considered previously by this house. I understand, too, that, in a general sense, it has been the opinion of the government that local advisory committees may function well in certain circumstances, and in others less well. My own inclination, Mr. Chairman, is to believe that with an active membership on the board itself the advantages of local advisory committees can be attained through this greater activity on the part of the members of the board without running into some of the disadvantages.

I agree with my hon. friend when he speaks of stereotyped or arbitrary management. I sincerely hope that the management, with the appointments we shall come to make if and when this legislation is adopted, will avoid anything that savours of that. I hope I made it quite clear when I first spoke to this resolution that I am most anxious not only that members of the board shall have numerous contacts with local authorities and local organizations, but that these should be as frequent and as friendly as possible.
The hon. member spoke also of the concern which exists in Montreal concerning the development of the harbour there in order to meet the changed conditions that will be brought about by the- seaway. I should like to say that I do not believe all this concern, which has been expressed by only a limited number of people in Montreal, is justified by the facts. I do not want to go into a long explanation concerning the seaway, but the question as to which side of the river the seaway was to be located upon was a very vital factor in the consideration by the national harbours board of the changes that would be made in the port of Montreal. The decision as to the location of the seaway was arrived at only recently, for reasons which I think it is unnecessary to go into now. I am advised, and I believe the advice I have given is sound, that we have adequate time to carry out the works that must be done, and the harbours board is fully conscious of the importance of carrying out those works.
A statement has been made recently that at the moment there is no accommodation in Montreal for long lake carriers, for the obvious reason they have been unable to get to Montreal and will not be able to get there until the navigation season of 1959. Then new facilities to accommodate them will be ready when the lakers are able to go to Montreal.
The hon. member referred also to the improvements in other ports. I believe that is covered by what I have already said, that I expect the board, by frequent visits and much local contact, to be fully acquainted with the changes that have become necessary in the various harbours under the board's control. Perhaps when the estimates of the harbours board are under consideration we may be able to go into that matter more fully, which perhaps is not of immediate concern.
The hon. member for Selkirk referred to the need for someone who knows the grain business. I might say that that suggestion has already been made to me. I feel it is a suggestion which has great merit. Perhaps the fact that the suggestion has been made indicates that not only are there these geographic

A great harbour such as that at Vancouver, or the one in Montreal, cannot be administered and developed by a board which has contact only very occasionally with that area. maintopic: HISTORIC SITES AND MONUMENTS ACT

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the work of the historic sites and monuments board has been drawing increasing attention across Canada during recent months, and particularly since it was formally establishd under an act on May 14, 1953. We welcome this resolution because it seems to indicate another step forward in the very important work of this group. The resolution indicates that by amending the Historic Sites and Monuments Act it is the intention of the government to further define the term "historic place", to change slightly the representation of the board, and to provide further for changes in the method and amount of payments to members appointed by the governor in council, of living and travelling expenses, and to provide for the payment of stenographic allowances. As I read the resolution, it seems to indicate that
1518	HOUSE OF
Historic Sites and Monuments Act it is the intention of the government to deal with one or two points that are required to strengthen the act.
Interest in Canada in the preservation of our historic sites has proceeded very slowly but this is to be expected because we are still a comparatively young country. One of the main weaknesses has been in the definition of what constitutes an historic place. Section 2 (b) of the act defines "historic place" as a site, building or other place of national interest or significance. Looking at that casually it would seem to cover most cases. However, there is a widespread feeling in the country that some sites of historic interest are not receiving their due consideration.
This point was raised in the findings of the Massey commission, particularly in reference to edifices or old buildings which are rapidly disappearing with the onset of commercialism in the modern day. For example, in Montreal there are many buildings and ancient edifices connected with the early days of Canada which have already disappeared. I hope that there is going to be an attempt made to deal more specifically with this problem.
On the other hand, there have been some notable achievements by the national historic sites and monuments board when it was acting as an honorary group. I refer particularly to the Champlain habitations on the shores of the Annapolis basin in Nova Scotia. These have been restored and provide a good idea of the manner of life in the new world at the beginning of the seventeenth century.
But there is a field of historic interest which antedates the coming of the white man to this continent. I refer to the period of Indian occupation of this great North American continent, particularly on the prairies. There are many sites there that could be regarded as of great historic value. I trust that amendments will be brought down which will enlarge the activities of the board in reference to these important places of antiquity. Up until recent years there were only 48 historic sites marked throughout the prairie provinces; 20 in Alberta, 20 in Manitoba and 8 in Saskatchewan.

In connection with the amendment of the definition of "historic place" there is another matter I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. More attention should be paid to buildings connected with early governmental activity in this country. The Massey commission referred to the original legislative building in Fredericton, New Brunswick, which at the time of the commission report had been partially demolished. There are many similar buildings scattered across the country. The tendency in recent years in preserving historic sites has been directed to those connected with more recent political activities. I feel that it is much more important that we go back to the beginnings of our national life as a Canadian nation and preserve some of these public buildings for posterity.
Then the second part of the resolution indicates that there is to be a slight change in the representation of the board. Section 3 (b) of the act gives the board the power to make agreements with any persons for marking or commemorating historic places pursuant to this act and for the care and preservation of any place so marked or commemorated. The amendment suggests that an attempt is being made to draw on the resources of voluntary groups throughout the country and to co-ordinate the work of various levels of government, each of which is vitally interested in preserving the historic sites and monuments in their particular territory.
Up to the present time there has been a degree of co-operation between federal, provincial and local levels^ of government. For example, the province of Ontario has done an outstanding job in restoring and preserving Fort Henry at Kingston. This part of the resolution seems to indicate that an attempt may be made to provide for further co-operation at these three levels of government.
There are historical societies scattered right across the country. Many communities are becoming keenly aware of the necessity of preserving the history of their local area. They lack guidance however as to what is truly significant. I know in my own province there has been an increased activity in this regard and just in the past few weeks I have received notices of the formation of several local historical societies which have been set up to preserve the history of their local areas and to mark the sites of historic interest in their particular sections. I trust that when the amendments come before the house they will indicate an attempt to assist the activities of these local historical societies, to give them some guidance which will help them to work closely with the board officially established by the act.

Finally, the resolution indicates that there is to be further allowance for travelling expenses, and also provision for the payment of stenographic allowances. One of the main difficulties in coming to grips with the problem of preserving our historic sites has been the lack of funds. I also feel that one difficulty has been the lack of a comprehensive policy and even of imagination on the part of those in responsible circles. I trust that the amendments to the act that will be brought forward will represent a long step in the direction of overcoming some of these deficiencies I have indicated.

For the more complete examination of the public accounts of the dominion, and for the reporting thereon to the House of Commons, the governor general may . . . appoint an officer, to be called the auditor general-

The main object of the bill was to carry that out, and inspire the public with confidence in the public accounts. It was deemed expedient, therefore, to adopt the English practice,-

maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 4, to regulate the exportation of power and fluids and the importation of gas.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the present bill is intended to replace an act that was placed on the statute books in 1907, that is, nearly

Power, Fluids and Gas half a century ago. The existing legislation, although it is not restricted to that field, has been associated in the public mind mainly with the policy of controlling the export of hydroelectric power. During the long course of its administration the export of fluids has come into the picture to some extent, especially in later years, but it is fair to say that until quite recently the act which is now being replaced has found its chief purpose and application in giving effect to the well defined attitude of the people of Canada toward the export of hydroelectric power.
Before dealing with the points in regard to which this bill differs from the provisions of the old act, I wish to refer, first, to some features of the advance of hydroelectric development in Canada, and also to some of the developments relating to Canada's gas and oil resources which have in late years placed the importance of those resources to the whole Canadian economy in an entirely new light. I shall also touch upon the policies affecting the administration of this legislation.
The production of electrical energy in Canada over the years has been a story of steady and rapid growth. When works now under construction are completed, by 1960, there will still remain in excess of 45 million horsepower for future harnessing. Happily a large amount of this potential power, which was formerly inaccessible in areas such as northern Labrador and the Yukon, should soon become accessible due to continued progress in the technique of long distance transmission of power at higher and higher voltages. A line now under construction in British Columbia will shortly be transmitting at 345,000 volts, which will be the highest transmission voltage on the North American, continent. Sweden at present is experimenting with transmission voltages in the order of 500,000 volts. These higher voltages, you will realize, mean much greater transmission distances, so the future picture is brighter than it has been for some time.
The question of export of electricity has been before the house on many occasions, with the principal debates commencing in 1907 when the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act was passed. Prior to 1907 some companies had undertaken the development of water power on the Canadian side of the border, and at that time an adequate market did not exist in this country for its total use. To render the projects economically feasible, contracts with United States firms were entered into by which blocks of power were transmitted to that country. The act of 1907 was passed to provide control over exports but was evidently not intended, in the earliest


years of its administration, wholly to preclude additional exports, since additional blocks were committed after that date. The general feeling at that time seems to have been that such export as was necessary to put the new power developments on a sound economic basis at their inception could be recalled at a later date as the need arose for its use in Canada.
This turned out to be fallacious. With this realization the policy firmed against export. On August 25, 1914, a minute of the privy council contained the following statement:
Power or energy generated from streams in Canada has been, as it must be, regarded primarily as a natural resource of the country to be developed and utilized to the utmost possible extent for the benefit of the country. And it was recognized that while it was consistent with that view to permit exportation so long as the demand in Canada for power should not be sufficient to absorb the whole production, yet it could be permitted only in such manner and on such terms as did not conflict with the ultimate necessity of security and preserving their natural resource for the use of the people of Canada if and when needed by them.
In 1925, when the subject of export was again to the fore, this house adopted the following resolution:
That the export of hydroelectric power from Canada should be permitted only on a yearly licence, and that hereafter no licence for export of power beyond that already granted should be issued except with the concurrence of the province or provinces in which it is proposed to develop such power.
In 1927-28 the house passed a bill, defeated in the Senate, which provided that the power which was then vested in the governor in council with respect to grants of licences for the exportation of electric energy, should be vested in parliament and not in the governor in council. That was the whole purport of the bill.
In 1933 the then prime minister made the following statement in this house:
We cannot afford to export power and create community life in another country with industrial activities and then, when the requirements of our own country call for cutting off the licence to export, contemplate that situation without having regard to a statement made by a president of the United States that such action on our part would practically be considered an unfriendly act.
In 1938 the House of Commons again dealt with the subject and passed a bill which prevented the issue of any new licence for the export of power unless it had been expressly authorized by a private act of parliament. This bill was not reported back by the other house.
While there have been differences of opinion as to how the policy on exports should be implemented, there is no doubt that such policy has crystallized in one of no firm commitment for power, that licences should

be on a surplus interruptible basis only, and that they should be reviewed annually.
Licences have been and are being issued for surplus interruptible power, and these together with the firm licences are reviewed before annual renewal. Applications are considered only for surplus interruptible power or for increases in existing surplus licences, and before any decision is taken it is cleared with the provincial government concerned. Finally, all export contracts of licensees must have attached to them copies of the export licence so that recipients of electric power from licensees may be fully aware of all conditions under which licences are granted.
May I turn now to the other resources to which the legislation relates. During the last few years since the oil discovery at Leduc in Alberta in 1947 there has been a continuous large and widespread exploration and development program in western Canada, which has resulted in the establishment of reserves of oil of approximately 2,750 million barrels, and reserves of natural gas probably in excess of 16 trillion cubic feet.
The market for crude petroleum has been extended by the building of pipe lines to the Pacific coast and to the Sarnia area in Ontario. These markets, together with the consumption on the prairies, resulted in 1954 in a production of approximately 95J million barrels, of which 88 million barrels were from Alberta, 5 million from Saskatchewan and 2 million from Manitoba. This is in contrast to a production of 6 [DOT] 8 million barrels in western Canada in 1947, the year of the Leduc discovery.
As a result of this large increase in production the rate of discovery has exceeded the market outlets. The potential production is now considerably in excess of the actual production. The refineries in the prairie provinces are now wholly supplied by crude oil from western Canada but it is unlikely, owing to geographical conditions, that all Canadian refineries will ever be supplied by Canadian oil. However, oil from the prairie provinces is now being exported to the adjoining areas of the United States and expansion in this respect may be expected in the future, particularly on the west coast.
In the course of the search for oil large quantities of natural gas have been found, particularly in Alberta and in the northeastern part of British Columbia, with smaller amounts in Saskatchewan. Natural gas has been supplied by pipe line to local centres of population in western Canada within economic reach of the gas fields. However, the reserves have grown so rapidly that there is urgent need for large markets. It is proposed to supply these by large pipe lines, 50433-97
Power, Fluids and Gas one of which is to be built from the Peace river area through central British Columbia to Vancouver and the adjoining Pacific northwest area of the United States, and the other from southern Alberta to supply central Canada, with a branch pipe line from Winnipeg south to the United States midwest. Sufficient gas is available and has been dedicated to these lines, and arrangements are now in preparation for their construction.
In 1954 there were more than 2,200 well completions in western Canada. Approximately 770 of these were exploration wells which were unproductive. The remainder were productive oil and gas wells. As a result of this drilling it has been estimated that there has been an increase in the gas reserves in western Canada of 4 trillion cubic feet and an increase in the oil reserves of about 600 million barrels.
In Manitoba in 1954 approximately 300 wells were drilled and the discoveries of oil have been most gratifying. There has however been no significant discovery of natural gas.
In Saskatchewan more than 700 wells were drilled during 1954 and a number of new discoveries of light oil were made. One of the important developments in Saskatchewan during 1954 was the arrangement made to market the medium gravity crude oil in the United States. Natural gas produced in Saskatchewan is now supplying a number of towns and cities, including Saskatoon, but sufficient volumes are not yet available to supply all provincial requirements. There is no doubt that with expanded markets the petroleum and natural gas industry in western Canada will continue to grow at a sufficient rate to meet all demands.
There have been many debates in this house on the policy which should be adopted for the export of oil and natural gas. The policy of the government with respect to oil was given to the house by the Minister of Trade and Commerce on March 13, 1953, and I quote from page 2928 of Hansard:
A distinction must be made between exports of petroleum and exports of natural gas. Petroleum is a commodity which moves freely across all international boundaries, as does iron ore, wheat and certain other basic commodities. The refiner buys his petroleum wherever he can buy it cheapest. He may buy today from Alberta, tomorrow from Venezuela, the next day from the Middle East and the next day from the United States, depending upon where he can make the best arrangement. No problem of continuous supply is involved. If one source becomes no longer available, the refiner may buy from another source. Petroleum can be moved in tanker ships, tank cars or tank wagons, and in such event its export from Canada is not under government control. In other words, as I have pointed out, petroleum moving in the manner I have just stated does not come under the provisions of the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act.
1526	HOUSE OF
Power, Fluids and Gas
Movement by pipe line is under government export control, but this does not alter the fact that there is no obligation imposed upon the government of Canada to maintain a continuous supply. Canada's national policy should therefore be, first, to move petroleum from the source of production to refineries within economic distance in the cheapest possible way; second, to arrange for markets for that portion of the Canadian output that cannot be economically used in Canadian refineries in the market that offers the highest return to the producer. This is the policy this government has followed and intends to follow.
Pursuant to that policy, the interprovincial pipe line has been built from Edmonton to Superior, Wisconsin, serving refineries at Moose Jaw, Regina and Winnipeg. The present route involves movement of the petroleum from Superior, Wisconsin to Sarnia, Ontario, by lake tankers. The entire movement from Edmonton to Sarnia is in bond, except for permits that have been granted to export small quantities of petroleum to the United States.
Interprovincial Pipe Line is presently engaged in extending this pipe line through the United States to Sarnia with the purpose of arranging for a continuous supply at Sarnia and further lowering the cost of transportation. The "in-bond" privilege presently granted to Interprovincial will apply to the new pipe line. This is consistent with government policy of approving the lowest possible cost of transportation from the source of supply to refining centres within economic distance of the source.
The policy of the government with respect to natural gas was expressed on the same day by the minister at page 2929 of Hansard, and I quote the pertinent section of that speech:
". . . Therefore the policy of the government of Canada is to refuse permits for moving natural gas by pipe line across an international boundary until such time as we are convinced that there can be no economic use, present or future, for that natural gas within Canada.
In brief, therefore, the policy with respect to these items is that export of oil should be based on the movement from the source of production to refineries in the cheapest possible way, and to arrange for that portion of the Canadian output that cannot be economically used in Canadian refineries the market that offers the highest return to the producer; that with respect to electricity there should be no firm export commitments and authorizations given only for interruptible surpluses; and that natural gas should leave Canada only when it is demonstrated to be surplus to determined Canadian needs.
With this background relating to the resources with which this legislation is concerned, and to the policies that are being followed, may I now direct attention to the main features of the bill. While this new bill has been introduced to replace the act of 1907, the principles underlying the former act remain largely undisturbed. Some changes which are proposed result from experience in the administration of this act over the years, and others from the broad developments which have been taking place


in the energy field, particularly since the questions of distribution of natural gas and petroleum products have assumed such a large place.
It is proposed to drop from this bill the existing requirement that applicants for export licences must obtain a licence to construct export pipe lines. The house will be aware that this is now a provision of the Pipe Lines Act, and there seems to be no necessity for duplicating the provisions of that legislation. No change, however, is being made in the existing law which requires applicants to obtain licences for the construction of transmission lines for the export of electricity.
In addition to a licence to construct export facilities, a person must have a licence which authorizes the volumes or quantities which may be exported through such facilities. Under present-day conditions it has seemed desirable to consider also what control should be exercised over the construction of import facilities and import volumes. The construction of lines for the import of oil is, of course, covered by the Pipe Lines Act, but in accordance with the policy I described earlier there does not appear to be any necessity for controlling import volumes.
In the case of electricity, two factors were considered. As any country is always anxious to obtain electric power, and as it is released by any country only under most stringent conditions, there seemed little purpose in requiring construction or import licences. However, in the case of natural gas it is common sense to assure ourselves that any import would be based on continuity of supply, and also to make certain that Canada's own gas resources can be developed in the most advantageous manner. For these reasons import control of natural gas and similar gases is being provided for. Construction of import gas pipe lines is, of course, covered in the pipe lines legislation.
Under the existing act the governor in council is empowered to impose, by proclamation, export duties not exceeding $10 per annum per horsepower on power exported from Canada, and not exceeding 10 cents per thousand cubic feet on fluids, including gas, exported from Canada. While an export tax of three one-hundredths of a cent per kilowatt hour, equal roughly to $2 per horsepower per annum, has been imposed since 1925 on electricity exported, no tax has ever been levied on the export of gas or other fluids. It is therefore proposed that the tax provision with respect to electricity be maintained, and that the tax provision with respect to fluids be dropped.
The house will be aware that in the various applications which have been heard by the

federal power commission in the United States this Canadian provision for a tax on natural gas has given rise to considerable concern. As the tax on fluids has never been imposed, and to give the necessary reassurance that it is not the policy of the government to impose one, its deletion is proposed. The house will have noted that in the corresponding section of the present act there is also authority to remove, reimpose or vary the amount of the tax. In view of the fact that similar authority has been provided under the Financial Administration Act, it is the view that it need not be restated in the present bill. The section with respect to exemption from tax has been removed, since any licensee in receiving a licence has given an undertaking to supply in Canada in any event.
The present act contains two sections covering revocation of licences. The new bill provides only one revocation section, under which licences may be revoked when a licensee has received notice of his breach of the terms or conditions of his licence and he continues to refuse or neglect to comply. I think it will be agreed that authority to export is a most valuable asset to any licensee, and that he would not knowingly place himself in the position of having this taken away. In these circumstances it is felt that the revocation clause as now provided will be adequate.
In the old act the section dealing with the question of surplus power leaves much to be desired. It is felt that this should be clarified. It is proposed to specify that "surplus" shall be that power which remains after due allowance has been made for distribution to customers for use in Canada during the period of the licence. In the case of electricity, power reserves for use in Canada are determinable on a day to day, week to week or month to month basis. Licences are therefore drawn on a maximum kilowatt rate, with an over-all annual kilowatt hour export rate. In practice, the only power that leaves Canada is that which is not immediately required for Canadian needs.
In the case of natural gas, "surplus" must of necessity have a different meaning. The house will recall that on April 15, 1953, at page 3881 of Hansard, the Minister of Trade and Commerce pointed out that the principal considerations in the construction and operation of any gas pipe line are: That sufficient gas must be transported for such periods as will permit the amortization of the capital costs of construction; that adequate and continuing deliveries of gas must be assured to distributors to enable them to underwrite the capital costs of distribution; and that adequate 50433-974
Power, Fluids and Gas and continuing supplies of gas must be assured to consumers. Therefore, in determining what shall be considered surplus, and so exportable, the governor in council in granting a licence for gas export will be guided by these considerations.
What will be done is that a thorough and complete review of the gas available to the applicant will be made. As accurate a determination of the requirements of Canada as is possible will also be made, so that during the term of the licence requested by the applicant there will be no possibility of the applicant being unable to meet any reasonable Canadian demand for service. Once the reserve position and the needs of Canadians have been established, the governor in council will be in a position to pass on the application for the remaining gas, any part of which he may determine to be surplus for the period of the licence.
I believe I have covered the major changes which are being placed before the house. In concluding, may I again state that in drafting the bill we have sought to retain the fundamental principles of the existing legislation, and to make only those changes which experience and new conditions indicate are required.

speechtext:
The present act gives very wide power to revoke a licence. That is contained in section 6, subsection 2, which reads:
Such licence is revocable upon such notice to the licensee as the governor in council deems reasonable in each case.

Power, Fluids and Gas
I do not suppose it would be possible to have a power of revocation much wider than the one contained in the present act. Then there is the power to limit exportation to the surplus after Canadian needs have been met, and also to regulate the price on export so that price will not be lower than the price charged to Canadian consumers. That power is very carefully set out in the present act, and in reading the debates which took place in 1907 when the act was first placed on the statute books one finds a reason for the precautions which were taken to ensure that Canadian requirements would be met before there was any export. For example, section 7 provides:
Any such licence may provide that the quantity of power or fluid to be exported shall be limited to the surplus, after the licensee has supplied for distribution to customers for use in Canada power or fluid to the extent defined by such licence, at prices and in accordance with conditions, rules and regulations prescribed by the governor in council.
Then there is subsection 2 which reads:
Every such licence is revocable at will by the governor in council if the licensee refuses or neglects to comply with any of the conditions imposed with regard to the supply and distribution of power or fluid in Canada.
There is also a regulation which will be found in an order in council passed on October 6, 1954, P.C. 1954-1522. I refer to clause 11, which reads as follows:
The price charged by any licensee for any electricity, petroleum or natural gas exported by him shall not be lower than the price at which electricity, petroleum or natural gas, respectively, is supplied by him or by his supplier in similar quantities and under similar conditions of sale for consumption in Canada.
One other feature of the present act to which I wish to refer is the power written into it to collect these export duties. That is contained in section 4 (a), and then there is section 4 (b), to which the minister referred, dealing with the right to remove or reimpose these duties or vary the amount thereof but which is not material for the purpose of my submission today.
There we find this in clause (c): exempt from the payment of such duties-
That is, the governor in council may exempt.
-such persons as comply with the direction of the governor in council with regard to the quantity of power or fluid to be supplied by such persons for distribution to customers for use in Canada.
There you find a precaution written into the legislation, again for the purpose of ensuring that Canadian consumers have the first chance at these commodities which were to be exported under licence.
As I have said, the act was first passed nearly half a century ago, in 1907. It was passed because the power potential of Niagara

falls was then being developed. The Conservative attitude at that time, as it has continued throughout and is today, was one of serving Canadians first. It was a Canada first policy. The members of the party to which I have the honour to belong believed then, as they believe now, that Canadians should be given the first opportunity to use their own resources. I have here a copy of the debates at that time, and the minister of justice summed up the purpose quite well, I think, in these words to be found in volume I of Hansard for 1906-07, column 1294:
The whole purpose of the legislation, as explained last year-
There had been legislation introduced the year before, I believe, but it had not become law.
-is not the collection of revenue alone, but the affording to the dominion authorities an efficient control over companies engaged in the production of power and the means of ensuring to the Canadian people the enjoyment of the great natural advantages which they have by reason of the wonderful water power at Niagara.
On the following page we find a reference to the imposition of duties, which is an important question. I shall take time to read it to hon. members.
If there is, under the provisions of this bill, found necessity to act. if any particular producer does not supply to Canadian customers the proportion of power which Canadian customers are desirous of having, and which it is reasonable he should supply, there is at once means to force his hand in that regard by imposing upon any power which that man seeks to export, a duty which will be practically prohibitive, a duty which would make it his interest at once to supply the Canadian demand first, and which would in that way secure to the people of this country the enjoyment of their own natural advantages. That, in brief, is the whole purpose of this legislation, and it has seemed after consideration that the means which we are here adopting by the proposal to issue licences on the conditions described, supplemented by the power to impose a duty if it should be necessary as a restriction upon an undue amount of exportation, is a way in which the desired end can be well accomplished.
This act has stood with very little change since it was passed in 1907. Recently, however, certain situations have arisen in Canada. For example, one of the companies incorporated to build a natural gas pipe line, namely Westcoast Transmission Company Limited, desired to bring natural gas down from the Peace river country through the central portion of British Columbia, and then export the surplus to the United States. When that company applied to the federal power commission at Washington for permission to do so, they found one obstacle was the fact that the licence given by Canada was too restrictive, and the power to revoke the licence was very wide. I believe those objections were raised in Washington.

Last year, as hon. members know, there was an attempt by Consumers' Gas Company of Toronto to import natural gas from the United States to serve the Toronto area. It was considered that the effect of such a move would be to make it impossible to have a natural gas pipe line across Canada wholly on Canadian soil. The act I am discussing contained no provision to control the import of gas.
Then, of course, there has been the trouble over the Columbia river development. We have heard a lot about that in the last few days. In addition, and I think perhaps of more significance in recent years the importance of water power, oil, natural gas, and uranium, which I think comes into the picture, has been increasing. These resources have now achieved an importance in Canada which can best be described as amazing.
Before I go on to deal with the manner in which Bill No. 4 meets these situations, I would ask that we call it six o'clock.
