maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I had just pointed out that in recent years four significant situations had arisen in connection with these resources of power, oil and natural gas. One of these was that the export licence issued by the dominion government had been found so restrictive that it was proving to be a handicap in connection with sales of Canadian resources. Second, there was no power in the old act to control the importation of natural gas, as distinguished from the exportation. Then I mentioned the trouble that had arisen over the development of power on the Columbia river. Finally I said that water power, oil, natural gas and uranium in recent years have assumed tremendous importance in the Canadian picture.
The bill does not purport to deal with the last two situations, but it does deal with the first two. We find that there is power to give much wider rights under a licence. It will no longer be possible for a licence to be cancelled arbitrarily. Then, too, the measure broadens the definition of "gas", and it provides for licensing control over the importation of that product. So in these ways it meets the first two situations to which I have referred.
In addition, as the minister mentioned, it removes the power to levy export duties on
Power, Fluids and Gas oil and gas, and also removes most of the powers to make sure that Canadian consumers have the first opportunity to use their natural resources. For example, though it takes away entirely the power to levy a duty on oil and gas, there still remains the power to levy a duty on electrical power, but the provision that an exemption may be granted from that duty, if Canadian consumers are given adequate supplies, has been removed.
It also removes the condition found in section 7 (1) of the existing act that the licence can set prices, in order that the Canadian consumer will have first call on these resources. It removes, too, the power to revoke a licence if Canadian consumers' needs are not being met.
I presume the regulations, to which I referred this afternoon and which also deal with prices, will expire with the old act, because a new set of regulations will have to be passed under the new act. There would appear to be only one direct protection left for the Canadian consumer, and that is the provision that a licence may-and I stress the word "may"; it does not say "shall"- require that the export shall be limited to the surplus after customers in Canada have been supplied.
We believe that the Canadian policy must be to secure to the people of Canada enjoyment of their own natural advantages. We ask that the minister give the assurance that that is the intention in the administration of this new measure. We believe such a policy is of vital importance to the nation, and becomes more vital every year as Canada develops and as the United States becomes shorter and shorter of many of her essential raw materials. The use in Canada provisions are more important now than ever. Yet they appear to have been weakened in this bill. It depends entirely, of course, upon what regulations are passed under the bill, and I think it would be much better if it were made obligatory to have this provision written into a licence. This afternoon the minister gave a definition of what would be considered surplus, dealing first with power and then with gas and oil. Perhaps he did not deal with oil, but he did deal with gas. The definition of surplus gas was different from the definition of surplus power. It may be that those definitions should be written into the act or into the regulations in some way. I did not gather from the minister's remarks whether it was intended that those particular definitions would be written into the regulations, and I suggest that consideration be given to some procedure of that kind.
I would remind hon. members that the United States has a very strict provision in

Power, Fluids and Gas its law. For example, in the natural gas act of that country the test which must be applied by the federal power commission before granting a licence to export gas is whether the proposed exportation or importation will be consistent with the public interest. And in practice this question, this test of public interest, has been interpreted in such a way that only surplus United States gas can be exported. Further, United States needs must come first. The gas which is being exported can actually be shut off if it should be proved at any time that there are existing needs in the United States adjacent to the line by which it is proposed to export the gas.
The bill meets some of these situations to which I have referred. But we believe that it should be considered only as a stop-gap measure. It does not go very far toward establishing a national energy policy for Canada.
When the minister was speaking he said he intended to deal with administration under the bill; and I took from his statement that he was going to state what administrative machinery would be set up. However, he said nothing along that line. The bill does not name any minister or any department to administer this legislation.
At present we have a very complex situation in the administration of measures of this kind, or measures having to do with the problem we are considering. For example, the Minister of Trade and Commerce issues licences under the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act. They are supposed to come under the standards branch of his department. I find that on page 66 of the annual report for 1953. On that page there is reference to the administration of the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act; yet in actual practice I understand that the expert on this question in the Department of Trade and Commerce is a Dr. John Davis, who is not in the standards branch at all but i& associate director of the economics branch.
Then the Canadian authority on oil and natural gas is Dr. George S. Hume of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. Water power comes under the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. The Pipe Lines Act is administered not by the Department of Trade and Commerce but by the Department of Transport. That department has little or no staff acquainted with pipe-line problems, yet there lies the administration of the Pipe Lines Act.
Another governmental body comes into the picture in the board of transport commissioners. They hear all the applications for permission to instal a pipe line; and


they, too, I believe have practically no staff trained to deal with those particular problems.
In so far as power is concerned, we now find the international joint commission exercising a great deal of authority. Certainly in connection with the Columbia river development that commission is the paramount body at the present time. I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether this situation is to continue under the new act, or is this new act the first step toward an adequate national energy policy with effective administrative machinery.
We believe there is great need for an over-all energy policy. Let us get away from dealing with the problem piecemeal, with different departments concerned. It is not an efficient way to deal with these important questions. For example, we suggest that consideration be given to setting up what might be called a national energy board, under which would be gathered a professional staff to deal with those questions, which would have the necessary information and the necessary training, and which could recommend policy to the government. Then once policy had been decided upon by the government, the board could implement that policy.
We have a similar board in the air transport board. It may be that there could be a national energy board with more independence than the air transport board has under present legislation; but it does seem that some such board would be very helpful in meeting the problems which will arise in connection with a national energy policy for Canada. Such a board could administer this particular bill that we are considering tonight. It could administer and advise on water power problems such as are bound to arise under Bill No. 3, which received second reading last night. This afternoon the minister mentioned the tremendous power potential in the Yukon and in Labrador. In connection with those developments there will have to be some proper administrative body here in Ottawa.
I believe that a board such as the one I have mentioned could very well do work of that kind, and also in the use of atomic energy for peacetime purposes. It is obvious now that in a few years Canada will be producing power from atomic energy. That will bring up a whole new set of problems, and some department is going to be required to accept the responsibility for dealing with those problems. They are all one form or another of national energy, and I believe a national energy board could very well meet the situation.

The big four in Canadian development in the years that lie ahead are in my opinion power from water, natural gas and oil, and power in the form of atomic energy from uranium.

speechtext: Don't forget coal.

speechtext:
Well, I will add coal as a fifth. I am afraid that the situation with regard to coal is a little more difficult. Each one of the four I have mentioned is easily transportable. This afternoon the minister said that power can now be transmitted for hundreds of miles. Oil can be carried for thousands of miles by pipe line, and so can natural gas. Power from uranium perhaps will be even more readily transportable than the other three forms. I hope it will be possible in a very few years to have power developed from atomic energy in those parts of Canada where there is little prospect of there being any other type of power. These big four will largely determine the location of industry and population in our country.
We believe the energy resources are among Canada's greatest assets, and that they can go far to make her one of the leading nations of the world. But if this is to be done we must get away from the present hit and miss method of dealing with those resources. We must have in Canada a national energy policy for the use of those resources, and the administrative machinery to carry it out. We believe that now is the time to get this done.
We support the bill as a half measure leading in the direction I have indicated; but we hope the government will move without further delay to take the other steps required to make those four wonderful resources fully available to the Canadian people in the most efficient form.

Mr. Speaker, may I first of all express my appreciation to the Minister of Trade and Commerce for the very lucid explanation he gave today which, to a greater extent than any other previous speech by the minister on this subject, has shown an awareness of the actual rate of growth of the western Canada gas and oil industry, and I think a greater appreciation than earlier speeches by the minister of the importance to the west and to this country of access to markets south of the forty-ninth parallel.
Further, I should like to say that I am in full accord with two sections of this bill dealing with the removal of controls on the export of natural gas. I shall explain my position with reference to those two points in a moment or two. On the other point, dealing with restrictions on the import of
Power, Fluids and Gas natural gas, I have only one thing to add. I have no objection to that move, but I feel that in the interests of the consumers of eastern Canada who are now using United States gas, any measures designed to place restrictions upon the import of that product should in fairness to those consumers be accompanied by steps by this government to ensure that on the cut-off of gas from the United States the eastern Canadian consumer is not going to find his bill jacked up by higher prices for gas from western Canada.
The minister pointed out in his address there has been some concern indicated in Washington during the last year or two before the federal power commission about restrictions on the export of gas from this country and the amendments he proposes to this act are designed to eliminate those objections. My only regret in this regard is that the minister and the government did not see fit, when this question was raised in the house some two years ago and repeated last year, to so amend this act as to give Canada a much better chance than it has had in the past two years to break into the markets of the United States northwest and middle-western states.
I might say that these amendments if passed are not going to offer any firm guarantee that Canada will be able to sell gas in the United States, but it is true to say that without these amendments we would have about as much chance as a snowball in hell of cracking any United States gas market. With these amendments the odds against the capture of the markets we must have in the United States have been greatly reduced. If these amendments are backed up by government policy which is a little more favourably disposed toward and a little more aware of the need of United States markets for Canadian gas, then I am sure in the next year or two we can capture certain vitally needed United States gas markets.
I should like to touch briefly upon a little past history in regard to this act. On March 31, 1953, there was a debate in this house in connection with Mid-Continent Pipelines Limited, at which time I made some comments concerning the question of the security of supply of gas brought into a country from a foreign source. I said, as reported on page 3471 of Hansard:

speechtext:
Could the minister assure us that he has given the United States an assurance that the

federal government will not impose an export tax during a sufficient period of time to ensure the amortization of the investment of the United States' side of the pipeline system?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have neither been asked to give nor have we given any such assurance. I suggest that my hon. friend is raising points with which the commission have not interested themselves up to date and I would hesitate to give any unsolicited commitments on these points.
Mr. Speaker, what did not appear in the record of the house was a comment I made to some of my colleagues when I left the chamber after that exchange with the minister. Outside of this chamber I commented that the fact that this government had not recognized the dangers of the campaign being fought in the United States against Canadian gas, the fact that this government had not seen fit to amend this act in such a way as to give the United States consumer a reasonable degree of security of supply and price, had sounded the end of any hopes of approval in the immediate future by the United States of the import of Canadian gas.
That prediction was borne out three weeks later, in June, 1954, when the federal power commission rejected the application of West-coast Transmission, and rejected the import of Canadian gas. The major reasons given were summed up in these words. In the absence of any intergovernmental agreement providing for a continuity of supply they, the F.P.C., dare not commit the northwest United States gas market to a foreign source of supply.
1 raise this point because I believe strongly that had the government seen these dangers earlier, had they recognized them-as I think perhaps I did at that time, because of the sources of information available to us in the publishing field out west-they would have taken action one or two years ago to remove the ground for arguments being voiced against Canada in the United States in order to ensure the capture of that market.
In March, 1954, Mr. Speaker, almost a year ago, the question first came up of the supplying of gas to the United States middle-western states. At that time the minister made certain statements. The minister made to the press a statement which I quoted in the house on March 30, 1954, along these lines, as reported at page 3494 of Hansard:
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) is a man of great talent, energy and bluntness. He has established a reputation for facing up to issues. I trust that he will, during this debate, face up in full to the facts regarding a Canadian gas policy. He did not face facts when he indicated to the press after the jperger of the Trans-Canada and Western pipe line companies that the line to eastern Canada had priority, that no gas would go to the United States until supply to our east was secured, and that gas would go to Minneapolis 50433-98
Power, Fluids and Gas
only on an interruptible basis. Surely he is fully aware of the various economic studies of the all-Canadian line to which I have referred.
This was on March 30, 1954.
Surely also he knows that the tying in of Minneapolis improves the economics of an ultimate line to eastern Canada, and that the large financial investment required by the Minneapolis company in order to take Canadian gas dictates that it must be a firm, not an interruptible supply.
That brings us up to date on these amendments. From the fact that he introduced these amendments I am sure the minister is now fully aware that United States consumers, just like Canadian consumers, when it comes to natural gas are concerned about security of supply and price. They must be so concerned, just like Canadians. After all, pipe lines involve extremely large capital expenditures for the transport pipe line and distribution pipe-line systems. In addition to that, every single customer using gas must make a sizeable investment in furnaces, stoves, gas heaters, water heaters and so forth, and naturally he must have a reasonable assurance that the supply of gas is going to be secure for some time to come.
I said earlier that by the passage of these amendments we do not ensure the capture of United States markets, but we change the outlook from one of hopelessness so far as getting those markets is concerned to one where we now have-if government policy changes along with the amendments to this ac't-a reasonable chance of capturing markets which are needed to support gas pipeline systems both east and west from Alberta.
I think it is now generally recognized by this government and by most members of this house that neither east nor west from Alberta can economically sound gas pipe lines be built if they are confined to Canadian routes and Canadian markets. We must have United States outlets served by both pipe-line systems in order to make a project which can provide a reasonable price to the producer, which can hold the price to the consumer down to a level he is willing to pay, and which can be built without soaking the Canadian taxpayer.
The minister made some references to the growth of the oil and gas industry. Among other things he stated that the gas reserves proved in 1954 in western Canada amounted to 4,000 billion cubic feet, or 4 trillion cubic feet were the words he used. In addition to that, oil reserves increased last year by some 600 million barrels. Then he went on with some estimates of current total reserves of oil and gas, I believe 2\ billion barrels of oil now proved and something like 16 trillion cubic feet of gas. I was glad to hear the minister use these particular figures, with one exception. I might
1534	HOUSE OF
Power, Fluids and Gas say that these figures originated in an article written by me two months ago, based on my usual year-end analysis of the oil and gas industry. I was happy to see that the minister places sufficient trust in the source to use those figures as being reasonably accurate.
The only figure he used which I disagree with was his figure of present proved gas reserves in the west. He stated the figure was something like 16 trillion cubic feet. The error there, sir, is that I think the minister used figures only for the province of Alberta. When we add something over 3 trillion cubic feet for northeast British Columbia and a thousand billion feet for Saskatchewan, the actual total proved reserve of gas in the west is now at least 20 trillion cubic feet.
Going a little further on this question of gas reserves, during the past three years-[DOT] and the source of these figures is the same as that of the figures quoted by the minister- western Canada gas reserves have increased by a total of about 12,000 billion cubic feet; in other words, an annual rate of 4,000 billion cubic feet in 1952, 1953 and 1954. This tremendous increase was partly due to discoveries incidental to oil exploration and partly due to exploration specifically made for natural gas, spurred by the hope that political controversy would end and markets for gas at fair prices would be opened up by the start of gas pipe-line development. How much more gas remains to be discovered no one of course knows for sure, but all geological authorities, including the authorities of this government, agree that the undiscovered reserves are many times those known today.
Western Canada has something over 700,000 square miles of geologically favourable territory for oil and gas, and this tremendous territory has so far been explored to an intensity of less than 5 per cent of the exploration to date in the major United States oil and gas regions. Huge reserves still remain to be discovered, but the rate of discovery will depend upon the degree of incentive provided. The best incentives, of course, are markets as fast as possible for the current shut-in reserves at prices that offer to producers some prospect of a reasonable profit. One year's gas discoveries, 4,000 billion cubic feet, are sufficient, I may say, to support and to serve the markets of one major pipe line for some 20 years.
Thus, during the last three years alone new gas reserves discovered have been adequate to support and service three major pipe lines for 20 years, but right now of course only two are proposed, one east and one west. So market planning is still not keeping pace with discoveries, and western Canada's gas surplus is continuing to grow. A single gas pipe line


east from Alberta, free to serve the economic and available markets in southern Saskatchewan and Manitoba, the Minneapolis area, northern Minnesota, Wisconsin and Michigan, plus the mass markets of southern Ontario and Quebec as far east as Montreal, could start off by selling less than 140 billion cubic feet of gas the first year of operation and might get up to some 200 billion cubic feet after five years of market build-up. At the western Canada gas discovery rate of the past three years, such an eastern pipe line serving both Canadian and United States markets would absorb less than 5 per cent of the gas reserves added to western Canada's total. A single gas pipe line west over the Rockies to serve British Columbia and the Pacific northwestern states could absorb little more than 100 billion cubic feet its first year of operation and might get up to 180 billion cubic feet by its fifth year. At the west's discovery rate of the past three years such a western pipe line would, in serving both Canadian and United States markets, absorb less than 5 per cent of gas added to reserves.
Thus the first two proposed major pipe lines, between them serving all really important Canadian markets along their routes between Vancouver and Montreal, and presently contemplated United States markets in the Pacific northwest, midwest and great lakes areas of the United States, would utilize only some 240 billion cubic feet their first year and perhaps up to 380 billion cubic feet by their fifth year. Based on the discovery rate of 4,000 billion cubic feet yearly, the two initial pipe lines would use their first year an amount equal to only about 6 per cent of the anticipated reserve growth that year and by the fifth year, assuming the same discovery rate, would use less than 10 per cent of reserve growth. If there is incentive to explore, there is every reason to expect no decline in reserve growth rate.
In the two years it would take to actually start construction and complete the proposed two initial pipe lines, additional reserves proved up might well amount to another 8,000 billion cubic feet, equal to the 20 years' needs of the two pipe lines, thus replacing in full the volume of reserves that would be dedicated now to get these pipe lines rolling. Even when these first pipe lines started operation their requirements for both Canadian and United States markets would amount to less than one-tenth of the anticipated discovery rate. In other words around 9 cubic feet of gas reserves would be added to the shut-in surplus for each one cubic foot used for the two initial pipe lines.
This figure of an accumulation of 9 cubic feet to shut-in reserves for every cubic foot

we would use with the two pipe lines operating compares with the picture of the last three years of some 30 cubic feet being added to the shut-in gas reserves of western Canada for every single cubic foot put to use in the markets of the prairie provinces. I think on the basis of gas reserve growth alone the government would be very well justified in going perhaps even a little further than the minister went today in planning a gas policy based not upon fear of shortage for Canada's long-term needs but rather a frank recognition that the problem is not one of shortage but of continually expanding gas reserves which are going to require not one pipe line each direction but a number of pipe lines within the next few years to absorb more than a small fraction of the reserves that are being developed. Obviously, sir, that makes more and more essential the capturing of outlets south of the border as well as those within Canada.
I do not think at this stage we should go into any detail as to government policy on pipe-line routes, but in view of some statements that have been made in the last few days by spokesmen for the government I think perhaps I should make some reference to a report which has been extensively quoted by these spokesmen in supporting the idea of the all-Canadian gas policy. Yes. It was on March 30, 1954, page 3496 of Hansard. The Stanford survey then took the next alternative, a Canadian-United States route but limited to Canadian markets and concluded that by the fifth year of operation, that is by the time the markets had been reasonably well built up, the Canadian-United States route would result in a transport cost of 2-8 cents per thousand cubic feet less than the all-Canadian route. On the basis of a trillion cubic feet of gas moved, there would be a saving of about $28 million.
The report then went on to consider the addition of United States markets, and stated that if the Minneapolis market were added to this pipe line the transport cost for all gas moved over the system by the fifth year would be reduced by another two cents a thousand. This again would represent a saving of $20 million per one trillion cubic feet.
The report then went further to deal with other possible United States markets in the great lakes area, added to or in lieu of the Minneapolis market, which would add another penny per thousand cubic feet in savings in transport costs, in other words a saving of another $10 million per one trillion cubic feet. The maximum saving in transport cost for a pipe line from Alberta to the east, the Stanford survey figures, by changing the route and by the addition of United States markets to those of the prairies and eastern Canada, would be 5-8 cents per thousand cubic feet or a mere matter of the equivalent of $58 million per one trillion cubic feet.
The market commitments to carry such a pipe-line system and finance it would total around 5,000 billion cubic feet for delivery over a 20-year period. In other words, using this Stanford survey the maximum possible saving on 5 trillion cubic feet would be about $290 million, to be shared by the producers and consumers in Canada. I believe it would

Dealing with the matter of price, since the minister brought it up, let us take a look at the Trans-Canada price, running east. Mr. Chairman, this act is administered in the Department of Trade and Commerce. All the talents of the department are brought to bear on any problem arising under the act. The standards branch have immediate charge of administering this act. The deputy minister's office, the director of economics and his associate director also study the act. Other departments are brought in if problems arise outside this department.
It is very difficult to gather up talent resting in persons with a good many other duties and put them in a department to deal with nothing but problems arising under this act, and similar problems. In Canada we have a limited but a very able and hard-working civil service. To take men out of various departments, put them into one branch or one body and say to them, "Your exclusive duties will be to administer the export of energy" would be, I suggest, a very wasteful way of using the talents of the men who have to do with the administration of these acts in the various departments where they serve.

With the international rivers authority being taken by the dominion government, many questions relating to power will have to be considered.
Would it not be a practical way of handling the matter if steps were taken to set up a national energy board along the lines of the

Power, Fluids and Gas air transport board? Under such a board experts would sit together and hear applications for permits under the Pipe Lines Act. Well, Mr. Chairman, a body of that kind would have perhaps no more than 10 applications every year- indeed, I would think 10 would be a large number-for the export of energy. Such a board would have to consist of very competent men, because the problems coming before it would be involved. Legal questions would arise, and there would be problems concerning which experience in the commodity would be essential.
Now, all that talent is available in the government service, talent of a very high order. It may be found in the international joint commission; it may be in the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, or in the Department of External Affairs. But wherever it is, it can be drawn upon to solve any problem that may present itself in connection with these export permits.
It seems that an ad hoc committee drawn from recognized experts in the government service is a method of meeting the situation much preferable to setting up a permanent board which would certainly not have enough problems to occupy its full time throughout the year. I have heard it suggested that the air transport board ties up a number of experts who have not a sufficient number of problems to occupy their full time. I do not agree with that view myself, because I think a specialized knowledge is being created in this board that is necessary in dealing with problems of air transport. But I do not think the problems of the export of energy are sufficient in number to warrant a permanent board of the type suggested by my hon. friend.

speechtext: I listened with interest to what the minister said about the ad hoc board and to his explanation about the various expert people who will be found in various departments, and it seemed to me good sense. Will the minister explain, or refer me to that part of the act which makes perfectly clear, how the ad hoc board to which he referred is to be constituted, and how it is to act?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext: We have today an interdepartmental committee on energy. Any matter having to do with energy is referred to that committee. It is not a committee established by act of parliament; it is simply a committee of civil servants who have duties relating to the field of energy. The Department of Trade and Commerce have to do with the exporting of energy, all energy, and the Department of Trade and Commerce are privileged to bring this committee together, to bring the experts together to discuss any problem of export of energy with which the department is confronted.

maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext: I suppose that would be in an advisory capacity.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext:
They are consulted. The decision rests with the minister of the department, who recommends the issuance of the permit to the governor in council. The governor in council of course is responsible for issuing any export permit for energy. But the minister has a responsible official who is a member of the committee on energy. He is able to consult his colleagues

on the committee, and the minister can rely on the fact that when he receives the report of his responsible officer he is receiving with it the consensus of the committee on energy consisting of civil servants of Canada.

maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext: Does this committee have anything whatever to do with an application before the board of transport commissioners for a permit to construct a pipe line?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext: No. The board of transport commissioners is a judicial body, as my hon. friend knows. Members of the committee appear before the board of transport commissioners and give the board the benefit of their views on individual applications. Mr. Davis, who has been referred to this evening, always appears for the Department of Trade and Commerce. When the question of crossing an international border is considered, Mr. Davis gives the views of the department as to whether crossing the border is in conformity with government policy. Other experts give their views on matters relating to the activities of the department to which they belong.

maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS

resources.

maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext: This is the clause which contains the only provision for protection of the customers in Canada. Will the minister deal with the plan he has in mind for making sure there is no relaxation from the course that has been followed under the old act, which does contain more stringent provisions dealing with this question?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext: I doubt whether the provisions are more stringent. The licences for the export of electricity are limited to one year. And we believe-

maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext:
That is a continuing feature?
Power, Fluids and Gas

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext: That is a continuing policy. We think the experts can determine whether there will be surplus power for the duration of that licence; that is, for the duration of one year. As my hon. friend knows, the only licences that are given for electricity are for surplus interruptible power. And the fact that it is interruptible is pinned to the licence. Therefore if at any time the power is no longer surplus the export can be cut off and the customer will have no recourse whatever. He simply buys interruptible power. So I think all the protection for Canadian consumers that anyone can reasonably require is provided. The condition is put in, if it is applicable, which it would be probably in connection with electrical current, that all Canadian consumers will be supplied before power can be exported. The regulations will provide that such a clause shall be inserted. I think it usually is inserted in power contracts.

maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext: What about the provision which is contained in the export act that the price to the United States consumer must not be lower than the price to the Canadian consumer? How is that going to be covered under the new bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext: There are very few cases where interruptible power that is exported competes with interruptible power sold in Canada. We assume that most utilities are owned by the provinces or by private companies. There is an export tax of $2 per horsepower on power exported, in any event, and whoever is responsible for recommending the licence could satisfy himself that power is not being sold out of Canada even on an interruptible basis at a lower price than interruptible power is being sold within Canada.

maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext: Is that written into the licence?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext:
The regulations do have a provision which reads:
The price charged by any licensee for any electricity, petroleum or natural gas exported by him shall not be lower than the price at which electricity, petroleum or natural gas, respectively, is supplied by him or by his supplier in similar quantities and under similar conditions of sale for consumption in Canada.

maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext: That regulation will be reenacted under the new act?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext:
The licence apparently refers to surplus power or surplus gas. For example, I have here the amended licence to West-coast Transmission Company Limited issued in April, 1953, and it refers to the export of surplus natural gas. The order in council authorizing that also contains those words.

Power, Fluids and Gas Just how do the minister and the department decide when power or gas is surplus and what power or gas is surplus? When the minister spoke this afternoon he gave a definition of surplus power and a definition of surplus gas. Are those definitions to be written into the regulations, or is this to be left to the judgment of the officials who issue the licence?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext: I suppose my hon. friend is referring to natural gas?

maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext: To both power and gas.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext: The province in which the supply is found issues a certificate. It allocates the gas for the purpose. It allocates that gas after it has determined that other resources within the province are ample to take care of the requirements of the province. Then the federal authority reviews the situation to make sure there are no markets within Canada that should be served or could be served economically as a deduction from the amount approved for export by the province. On the basis of that it is determined that a certain amount safely can be allowed to go to export. We are dealing there with a commodity where the supply is constantly expanding, and we expect that to be the case for a good many years. So I think it is necessary to take the expert opinion of the officers, both the responsible officers in the province where the gas originates and the responsible officers in the federal government who advise the government on matters of that kind.

maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext:
I think the
minister mentioned a moment ago that none of this gas or electricity would be exported except on an interruptible basis.

maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext: I was speaking of electricity. I said that electricity is always exported under a licence good for one year only and on an interruptible basis. It is impossible to sell gas-

maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext: Of all contracts that have been made within about the last 15 years. Some of the early contracts made before the first world war were not on an interruptible basis, and it was the experience of that early practice that brought about the more recent plan of selling electricity on an annual basis and under an interruptible contract.

maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext:
That would not apply to the export of gas?
Mn Howe (Port Arthur): No, it cannot. The reason is that there must be a continuity

of supply in the case of gas. It would be impossible for a utility to rely on gas from a source which was interruptible. In the case of gas we have to assess the situation to make sure that we have gas surplus to the requirements of Canada, either present or future.

maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext: I am glad the minister has given that explanation. As I listened to him I just could not understand how any contract could be entered into, particularly for gas, on an interruptible basis. The minister assures us that that is not the case, but if it were the case it would simply be a prohibition on the export of gas.

maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext: This afternoon I understood the minister to give definitions of what constituted surplus power and surplus gas. Is that merely a rule of thumb that is followed in the department, or is it to be set out in the regulations?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext: It is the policy of the department. It would be impossible to set this out in the regulations. The policy is a guide to those who recommend to the minister that a licence be issued. It is a definite policy, and has been so for many years.

maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext: Would it not be wiser to have it set out in the regulations so there would be legal effect to it? The way it is now I presume that it could be changed at a moment's notice. It really has no great effect when it is simply a type of directive. Would it not be an advantage to have it set out in the regulations?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext: No, I think it could hardly be set out in the regulations. That is the pattern on which the particular facts applying to an application are judged. Each application is considered on its own set of facts and is measured against the yardstick of departmental policy. The recommendation is made accordingly. To have a set of principles set out in the regulations and then have judgments made on the facts of the case might lead to legal difficulties in subsequent years. I think the department must be responsible for recommending each individual permit.

maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext: In effect each case is dealt with separately and on its own merits rather than being based on a general rule or general regulation?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext: That is correct.

Subject to the regulations and to such terms and conditions as the governor in council may approve with respect to each licence, licences may be granted for-

maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce

speechtext: That is correct.

maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: POWER, FLUIDS AND GAS LICENSING CONTROL OVER EXPORTATION OF ELECTRIC POWER AND FLUIDS, AND IMPORTATION OF GAS
speechtext: That is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
We ran out of
business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Oh, no; I announced that we would take all the rest of the resolutions on the order paper. On Monday we shall begin with the resolution in the name of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) with respect to the Railway Act and the railwayhighway crossing problem.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I wonder whether that resolution could be allowed to stand over and not be taken on Monday? I refer to the grade crossing resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Then we shall take the one in the name of the Minister of Transport with respect to loans to the New Westminster harbour commissioners; the resolution with respect to the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act; the resolution in the name of the Minister of Labour with respect to the Government Employees Compensation Act; the one in the name of the Minister of Finance with respect to the Public Service Superannuation Act, and then the two in the name of the Minister of National Revenue with respect to double taxation and our treaty with Ireland.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 9.44 p.m.

Monday, February 28, 1955
